tldr: The authors propose a framework that selectively collects weakness data by detecting discrepancies between human demonstrations with a handheld gripper (UMI) and policy inference in real time, without running a physical robot. It demonstrates significantly higher learning and collection efficiency than conventional SFT and teleoperated intervention methods (HG-DAgger) across real-world tasks.
hero_caption: Overall pipeline of HIL-UMI. While a human works with a handheld gripper, the policy and advantage estimator run inference in real time in the background. The system uses metrics like the Energy Score to detect and collect out-of-distribution (OOD) data and low-progress segments where the model struggles, and efficiently runs iterative post-training via ACBC.
overview:
Large-scale vision-language-action (VLA) models provide powerful priors, but post-training is essential to adapt them to a specific robot and environment. However, supervised fine-tuning (SFT) that simply imitates static demonstrations cannot prevent compounding errors when slight mistakes lead the robot into unvisited out-of-distribution (OOD) states. It also cannot distinguish which data actually contributed to task completion.

Human-in-the-loop approaches like DAgger address this, but they require humans to teleoperate and correct errors while running a physical robot. This is very hard to scale due to hardware preparation, safety concerns, and workspace constraints. To solve this, the authors turned to the Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI), which enables demonstrations using an inexpensive handheld gripper, and proposed HIL-UMI: a system that collects policy-guided data to reinforce weaknesses without executing a physical robot at all.

While a human demonstrates tasks, the current policy runs concurrently on the camera video stream. The Energy Score evaluates the discrepancy between the human demonstration and the policy prediction distribution in real time. Additional data is collected intensively only when encountering model weaknesses with large discrepancies. The model is then iteratively updated via advantage-conditioned behavioral cloning (ACBC) combined with an advantage estimator that predicts task progress.

Evaluations on four challenging real-world tasks, including folding towels and organizing drawers, showed that HIL-UMI consistently outperformed SFT under the same data budget. Furthermore, compared to physical-robot teleoperated interventions with HG-DAgger, HIL-UMI achieved higher task progress scores while speeding up per-frame collection time by about 5.6x.
contributions: Built a novel framework enabling policy-guided human-in-the-loop post-training using a handheld UMI without physical robot execution.
Proposed an out-of-distribution (OOD) detection method that evaluates the discrepancy between human action chunks and policy probability distributions in real time using the Energy Score.

Established an iterative learning loop that collects online data to update weaknesses in the progress-based advantage estimator itself, prioritizing optimal actions via advantage-conditioned behavioral cloning (ACBC).
Demonstrated superior task completion and higher data collection efficiency over SFT and real-robot HG-DAgger across four real-world manipulation tasks spanning long-horizon and precise operations.

sections.heading: Targeting Model Weaknesses Without a Physical Robot: A New Post-Training Approach
sections.summary: Adapting VLA models to real environments benefits from human-in-the-loop methods to overcome static SFT limits, but physical robot execution costs have been a bottleneck. This paper proposes HIL-UMI, which uses a handheld gripper (UMI) to target and collect policy OOD states without using physical robots.
sections.details:
Large vision-language-action (VLA) models offer general manipulation capabilities, but post-training is essential to adapt them to specific environments and arm characteristics. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT), which directly imitates human demonstrations, is widely used for this purpose. However, SFT faces two persistent challenges.

The first is covariate shift and compounding errors. Static demonstrations only cover successful paths. If the policy makes a small mistake and enters an out-of-distribution (OOD) state, it cannot recover. The second is that SFT treats all data equally, failing to distinguish which actions truly contributed to task progress.

To address this, methods such as DAgger and RECAP have been proposed where humans intervene via teleoperation when the policy fails. However, these require humans to stand by and intervene while physical robots are in motion. This poses major hurdles: safety risks, occupied hardware, and difficulty scaling parallel data collection across multiple operators and locations.

This work turns to the Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI), which collects robot-compatible data using a portable handheld gripper. While a human demonstrates tasks by hand, the observation stream is simultaneously fed to the background policy, detecting moments when policy predictions strongly diverge from human actions. In other words, HIL-UMI achieves highly efficient and scalable human-in-the-loop learning by correcting only where the model struggles, all without running the robot.

captions.F2: Overall view of HIL-UMI. As a human operates the UMI, the advantage estimator and policy run real-time inference in the background. Data in challenging out-of-distribution (OOD) regions exceeding a threshold are selectively recorded and used to iteratively train the model.

sections.heading: How Does It Differ from Prior Work? Merging Robot-Free Collection with Active Interventions
sections.summary: Conventional VLA post-training relies on physical robot teleoperation or interventions, while UMI research has focused mainly on sensor fidelity and passive collection. HIL-UMI stands apart by leveraging UMI's portability to actively collect weakness data linked to the current policy's predictions.
sections.details:
Related work broadly spans two areas: VLA post-training / interactive policy improvement, and robot-free data collection using UMI.

### II-A VLA Post-Training and Interactive Policy Improvement
To overcome SFT limits, several methods have been developed: DAgger provides human corrections on states visited by the learner; HIL-SERL combines real-robot RL with human intervention; and RECAP trains on real-robot experience and teleoperated corrections using advantage conditioning. However, all these approaches ultimately rely on humans intervening while physical robots are running. Consequently, collecting data across many operators in parallel for long-horizon or high-precision tasks has been very difficult.

### II-B Robot-Free Data Collection with UMI
UMI emerged as a way to collect manipulation data without physical robots using a portable gripper. Subsequent works such as multi-camera MV-UMI and high-precision HiFi-UMI have enabled data quality comparable to real robots. However, real-time feedback in existing UMI research has been limited to passive quality control, such as checking camera field-of-view or capture quality. They did not collect data based on what the current policy struggles with.

### II-C UMI-Based Human-in-the-Loop Post-Training
Recently, methods like RoboPocket have visualized predicted policy trajectories for human correction, while EgoGuide fills unexplored regions based on visual novelty. However, RoboPocket relies on subjective human judgment of weaknesses and does not consider data utility. EgoGuide does not guide collection based on the policy's own predictive distributions. HIL-UMI objectively detects weaknesses through statistical discrepancies in trajectory predictions and pairs them with an advantage model of task progress, achieving data collection and training truly tailored to the policy.

sections.heading: How HIL-UMI Works: From Weakness Detection to Advantage-Conditioned Learning
sections.summary: When a human operates UMI, the policy is inferred multiple times in the background to detect discrepancies (OOD) in real time using the Energy Score, collecting weakness segments. Simultaneously, segments where the advantage model struggles to predict task progress are collected and updated, and ACBC emphasizes high-value actions during training.
sections.details:
In each post-training round, HIL-UMI collects two types of data under the same frame budget: policy improvement data ($\mathcal{D}^P_r$) and advantage model update data ($\mathcal{D}^A_r$).

### III-A Online Data Collection and OOD Detection
Here, OOD refers to states where model predictions diverge from human demonstrations.

1. **Policy Data Collection**: For human observation $o_t$, the policy performs stochastic inference $N=10$ times concurrently to form an empirical distribution of predicted action chunks. To measure the discrepancy between human action chunk $H_t$ and the policy's predictive distribution, the Energy Score is computed. Its first term measures average distance between the demonstration and predicted samples, while the second term subtracts the variance among predicted samples. This captures both distribution spread and center shift rather than simple pointwise error. When this score exceeds threshold $\tau_P$, the state is deemed a policy weakness, and the demonstration trajectory from the current state to subtask completion is recorded.

2. **Advantage Data Collection**: An advantage model $f_\psi$ evaluates progress between observation pairs separated by $K$ frames online. If the predicted value falls below threshold $\tau_A$ despite the human making task progress, the estimator is considered to underestimate progress. This failure case is likewise recorded until subtask completion.

### III-B Advantage Model Training
Predicting progress from the difference of two independent states easily accumulates errors. Instead, the method trains a model that predicts relative progress directly from observation pairs $(o_u, o_v)$. To maintain consistency across partial segments with varying lengths, a linear progress target normalized by average episode length $\overline{L}_0$ is assigned. The model is updated by balancing past data and new round data.

### III-C Policy Update via Advantage-Conditioned Behavioral Cloning (ACBC)
The updated advantage model evaluates each sample in initial dataset $\mathcal{D}_0$, assigning positive (1) labels to the top 30% ($\eta=0.3$) and negative (0) labels to the rest. In contrast, newly collected policy data in the current round targets weaknesses and is all labeled positive. These labels are appended as prompts to the policy's language instructions for training (ACBC). At inference time, conditioning on the positive prompt ensures the model consistently chooses actions that contribute significantly to task progress.

sections.heading: Real-Robot Validation: Outperforming SFT with 5.6x Faster Collection than HG-DAgger
sections.summary: Experiments were conducted on four real-world tasks using a Franka arm. HIL-UMI showed substantial gains over SFT, and ablations confirmed the importance of the advantage model and detection thresholds. Compared to physical teleoperated interventions (HG-DAgger), HIL-UMI achieved higher scores while accelerating collection time by about 5.6x.
sections.details:
### IV-A Hardware Setup
The handheld device uses a custom UMI connecting a Meta Quest 3 controller to an AgiBot OmniPicker gripper via a custom connector. Tracking runs on the Meta Quest 3 system, and observations are captured at 30 Hz from a gripper camera (Intel RealSense D405) and a fixed third-person camera (D455). Parallel inference on an NVIDIA RTX 4090D workstation achieves low-latency online operation: 112 ms for policy OOD detection and 93 ms for advantage OOD detection.

### IV-B Real-World Tasks and Results
Using a Franka Panda arm, the open-source $\pi_{0.5}$ policy was fine-tuned and evaluated on four tasks (two long-horizon, two precise):
- **Fold Towel**: Unfold a randomly placed towel, smooth wrinkles, fold it twice, and place it in a basket (long-horizon).
- **Clean Up Table**: Open a drawer, sort pens, and store toys in another drawer (long-horizon).
- **Stack Cube**: Grasp a purple cube and precisely stack it on top of a red cube (precise).
- **Stamp**: Grasp a stamp and stamp precisely inside a printed outline on paper that is only 1 cm larger than the stamp (precise).

Initial object placements were varied across a $30\text{ cm} \times 60\text{ cm}$ area, measuring task progress score (TPS) from 0 to 100. While conventional SFT plateaued or degraded as more data was added, HIL-UMI consistently improved TPS across rounds.

### IV-C Ablation Studies
- **Role of the Advantage Model**: Removing the advantage model and using standard fine-tuning caused a sharp drop in performance because the model could not distinguish high-progress actions.
- **Threshold Sensitivity**: Varying thresholds $(\tau_P, \tau_A)$ on Stack Cube showed that overly loose thresholds collected unhelpful data, while overly strict thresholds missed useful failures. The balanced intermediate setting (1.2, 0.2) was optimal.

### IV-D & IV-E Collection Efficiency and Comparison with HG-DAgger
Because per-frame filtering takes time, HIL-UMI's recording time per frame is slightly longer than standard SFT. However, because it avoids redundant data, TPS gains relative to cumulative collection time were dramatically superior. Furthermore, when compared on Clean Up Table against HG-DAgger (which uses physical robot teleoperation for human intervention), HIL-UMI achieved about 5 points higher TPS. Notably, HG-DAgger required 412.99 ms per frame, whereas HIL-UMI required only 73.40 ms, representing a 5.63x speedup in data collection efficiency.

sections.heading: Summary and Outlook: Toward Scalable Robot Learning Free from Physical Robots
sections.summary: This study proposed HIL-UMI, which detects policy weaknesses and trains with advantage estimation on a handheld UMI without physical robots. Looking ahead, this approach points toward distributed robot learning systems where multiple operators in different locations collect weakness data simultaneously.
sections.details:
This paper proposed HIL-UMI, a novel human-in-the-loop VLA post-training framework that requires no physical robot rollouts.

While a human operates naturally with a handheld gripper (UMI), the system evaluates the gap between policy predictions and human actions in real time via the Energy Score to pinpoint weakness data. It concurrently updates an advantage estimator of task progress and trains using ACBC. This design prevents the data collection plateaus seen in standard SFT, delivering consistent performance gains across precise and long-horizon tasks.

For future work, the authors highlight extending this system to distributed environments. Because it does not tie up physical robots, operators around the world could collect weakness data simultaneously using handheld devices to continuously improve a central, large VLA model. As a scalable post-training method liberated from physical robot constraints, this is a very exciting direction for future research.

takeaways: Out-of-distribution (OOD) data can be accurately collected without moving physical robots by feeding human demonstration video to the background policy in real time and measuring discrepancies with the Energy Score.
Simply adding more demonstrations via SFT quickly hits performance plateaus, but targeting weakness regions significantly improves performance under the same data budget.
Training an advantage estimator online alongside the policy and applying ACBC enables the model to prioritize actions that genuinely drive task progress from the collected data.

Data collection time is reduced by more than 5x compared to real-robot teleoperated interventions like HG-DAgger, offering strong scalability for parallel collection across multiple operators and locations.
limitations: Initial tuning of the thresholds ($\tau_P, \tau_A$) used for Energy Score and advantage evaluation is required, and extreme values reduce collection efficiency or learning performance.
Because human operators interrupt tasks to provide additional demonstrations at the subtask level, the process depends on operators having some understanding of the task structure.
Slight physical dynamics discrepancies between the handheld gripper and the physical robot arm mechanism could affect tasks requiring extreme contact-force control.
